articles.body:
## Scope

A reported zero resistance is an operational result: the voltage is below the detection threshold for a specified current and contact geometry. The experiment establishes a bound on resistance rather than a mathematical proof that it is exactly zero. This article concerns electrical transport; magnetic expulsion and thermodynamic anomalies require separate measurements. The superconducting condensate provides the theoretical setting, but a microscopic model does not replace the experimental controls. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

Record resistance onset, midpoint and zero separately. An onset can identify a small superconducting region, whereas a connected path may determine the zero-resistance result. Neither number alone measures the superconducting volume fraction. Filaments, an interface or a second phase can dominate a four-terminal path even when most of the specimen remains normal. This distinction is central when comparing bulk crystals, films and high-pressure samples. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a measured voltage resolution $V_{\mathrm{res}}$ and applied current $I$, an unresolved voltage implies the operational bound

$
R_{\mathrm{meas}} < \frac{V_{\mathrm{res}}}{|I|}.
$

This expression is a measurement definition, not a universal material law. It assumes a meaningful current path, stable contacts and a noise floor evaluated under the actual acquisition conditions. In a homogeneous specimen, converting resistance to resistivity further requires the sample dimensions. The ideal condensate response is a limiting statement about frequency, temperature, field and current; a finite experiment cannot take every limit simultaneously. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## Experimental criteria

Use four-terminal measurements and show the raw resistance-versus-temperature or voltage-versus-current data. Report excitation current or current density, voltage threshold, field direction, sweep direction, contact arrangement and sample history. Repeat measurements at different currents to distinguish a robust transition from heating, a contact short or an instrument floor. For a claim of bulk superconductivity, seek independent magnetic or thermodynamic evidence. These are editorial evidence requirements, not a claim that one universal protocol fits every apparatus.

Halperin and Nelson developed a vortex-unbinding description of resistive behavior in dirty superconducting films, including fluctuation conductivity above an effective vortex-unbinding temperature and nonlinear resistivity below it. This is a theoretical treatment of a specified film regime, not a measurement of pairing symmetry. When applying it to data, this article requires independent checks of the model assumptions and sample conditions; a fit alone is not treated as a unique diagnosis. The publisher abstract supports this limited description; its full derivation has not yet been reviewed here. [R2](#ref-source-9e55a4505d9de546)

## Limits and disputes

Light-driven optical signatures must remain in a different evidence category from an equilibrium transport transition. Mitrano and colleagues reported a transient superconducting-like response in driven K3C60. The source chapter itself retains the ambiguity of assigning superconductivity from optics alone. Budden and colleagues investigated a longer-lived driven state with transport observations; those observations do not define an equilibrium zero-resistance critical temperature. This pilot does not promote either optical scale into a bulk temperature ranking. [R3](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1) [R4](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690)

A persistent current can be complementary evidence, but its interpretation needs the loop geometry and decay time. A single low-resistance reading cannot supply those quantities. Likewise, magnetic-field suppression supports a superconducting interpretation without uniquely identifying the pairing interaction. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## Discovery implications

Treat zero resistance as one part of an evidence chain. A useful candidate report specifies a measurable threshold, demonstrates repeatability and connects transport to other probes. Preserve negative controls and the possibility of a minority superconducting path. This approach makes a discovery claim more testable while keeping unresolved volume fraction, phase identity and mechanism explicitly open. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R2](#ref-source-9e55a4505d9de546)

## Related topics

Read [Meissner evidence](/scwiki/meissner-effect) for magnetic tests, [two-dimensional and interface superconductivity](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces) for phase coherence, and [Planckian dissipation](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation) for normal-state transport inference.

Meissner and Ochsenfeld's historical observation of flux expulsion is conceptually different from merely freezing the field already inside an ideal perfect conductor. Electrical transport and magnetic response therefore answer complementary questions. A sample may screen a changing field while retaining trapped vortices, so the cooling protocol must accompany a magnetization curve. Separate zero-field-cooled shielding, field-cooled magnetization and magnetic hysteresis. Strong pinning can make the field-cooled signal small even in a superconducting specimen. Conversely, a large shielding response cannot be read as an exact superconducting volume fraction without considering shape, connectivity and background subtraction. The magnetic inference belongs to the actual sample and protocol, not to a chemical formula in isolation. [R2](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

## Mathematical assumptions

The local, homogeneous London description gives

$
\nabla^2\mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf B}{\lambda_L^2}.
$

The penetration depth $\lambda_L$ describes the decay of magnetic field in the stated limit. In a simple single-component convention, $\lambda_L^{-2}$ is proportional to superfluid weight. Multiband, anisotropic or non-local electrodynamics requires a more careful response model; the same fitted depth need not represent the same microscopic density across those settings. For an approximately ellipsoidal specimen, the measured susceptibility is altered by a demagnetizing field. The correction depends on the field direction and shape. Bulk claims benefit from consistency with transport and thermodynamic measurements rather than one isolated diamagnetic trace.

articles.body:
## Scope

BCS theory provides a microscopic pairing framework and a useful weak-coupling reference point. This article concerns its equilibrium, single-band, isotropic implementation with a smooth density of states and an effective attraction near the Fermi surface. Those assumptions define a model, not a classification of every superconductor. Agreement with one numerical ratio does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

The Cooper problem asks what happens when two electrons interact above an otherwise inert, filled Fermi sea. In the idealized attractive-shell model, a bound pair exists below the two-particle continuum for arbitrarily weak net attraction. The filled sea and its excluded states are essential to this result. It is not a claim that every attractive potential binds two isolated electrons in vacuum, nor is the two-electron calculation alone a construction of the finite-density superconducting state. [R2](#ref-source-d0ec754310a67e88)

## Mathematical assumptions

Write the attractive matrix element as $-V$, with $V>0$. Let $N(0)$ count states of **one spin** per unit energy, using the same volume normalization as $V$, so $\lambda=N(0)V$ is dimensionless. The energy cutoff is $E_c=\hbar\omega_c$, where $\omega_c$ is an angular frequency. With $\xi$ measured relative to the chemical potential, the excitation spectrum and gap equation are

$$
E(\xi)=\sqrt{\xi^2+|\Delta|^2},
$$

$$
1=\lambda\int_0^{E_c}\frac{\tanh[E(\xi)/(2k_BT)]}{E(\xi)}\,d\xi.
$$

The positive-energy integral already accounts for the symmetric negative-energy interval in the momentum-sum formulation. Inserting a two-spin density of states without changing the prefactor doubles the effective coupling. At zero temperature this model gives $\Delta_0=E_c/\sinh(1/\lambda)$. For $\lambda\ll1$, the usual limiting forms are

$$
k_BT_c\simeq\frac{2e^\gamma}{\pi}E_c e^{-1/\lambda},
$$

$$
\frac{2\Delta_0}{k_BT_c}\simeq2\pi e^{-\gamma}\simeq3.528.
$$

Here $\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant; $2e^\gamma/\pi\simeq1.134$. These are model results, not a measured transition temperature. We use modern $\Delta$ notation for the single-quasiparticle threshold; creating two quasiparticles costs at least $2\Delta$ in this idealized spectrum. The original paper used different notation and rounded numerical estimates. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## Experimental criteria

A useful comparison needs a gap measurement and a separately specified superconducting transition criterion on a comparable sample. Report whether the measured quantity is a single-particle threshold, a pair-breaking energy or a fitted spectral parameter. State temperature, magnetic field, sample composition and uncertainty before calculating a gap ratio. A peak separation must not silently be substituted for $\Delta_0$.

Then compare more than one observable: the temperature evolution of the gap, electronic thermodynamics and magnetic response constrain different aspects of the state. Distinguish a consistency test of the isotropic weak-coupling model from evidence for a particular microscopic mediator. No sample-specific $T_c$ or gap value is added to the material-comparison catalogue by this theoretical article. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## Limits and disputes

The general pairing construction should not be equated with a universal weak-coupling phonon mechanism. A frequency-dependent interaction, several coupled bands, an anisotropic gap or a rapidly varying density of states requires a more suitable equation. Phase fluctuations can also separate a pairing scale from the temperature at which long-range or quasi-long-range coherence develops. The simple gap equation above does not calculate that fluctuation problem.

The familiar isotope exponent $-d\ln T_c/d\ln M=1/2$ follows only if the cutoff has harmonic mass scaling and the remaining effective parameters are mass-independent. Changes in structure or coupling invalidate that inference. Likewise, a nonstandard gap ratio can motivate tests of stronger coupling or anisotropy; it does not, by itself, prove a named alternative mechanism. These applicability cautions follow the scope of the pinned B1 source chapter and are not new experimental findings. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## Discovery implications

Use BCS as a controlled baseline: define the band model, interaction window and normalization before fitting. Check that the inferred scales fit within the regime assumed by the calculation, rather than extrapolating an exponential formula into a flat-band or low-density regime. Compare alternative explanations using measurements that distinguish them. In particular, finding a Cooper instability is a starting point for a many-body theory, not the final demonstration of a material's phase coherence or pairing mediator. [R2](#ref-source-d0ec754310a67e88)

A productive research record should retain which assumption failed, which observation exposed the failure and which additional measurement could decide between the remaining models. This is editorial guidance for using the baseline, not a claim of an experimentally established route to higher $T_c$.

## Related topics

Connect the model to [zero-resistance evidence](/scwiki/zero-resistance), [the Meissner effect](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [two-dimensional coherence](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces).

articles.body:
## Scope

Multiband pairing concerns how superconducting gaps on distinct bands are coupled. Multichannel pairing concerns different interaction contributions to a Cooper-pair kernel. Neither concept is equivalent to parallel normal-state electrical conductivities, and neither means that two spatially separate superconducting phases form one homogeneous condensate. Keeping these distinctions explicit prevents apparent evidence for several channels from becoming an unsupported mechanism claim. [R1](#ref-source-e6ac5c48a0e11fe3) [R3](#ref-source-d7ac492f79e0915b)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a simplified weak-coupling model with a shared cutoff energy $E_c$, a linearized gap equation can be written

$
\Delta_i=L(T_c)\sum_j\lambda_{ij}\Delta_j,
\qquad
L(T_c)=\ln\!\left(\frac{1.13E_c}{k_BT_c}\right).
$

In this declared approximation, the largest relevant pairing eigenvalue sets the instability. Off-diagonal entries represent interband pair transfer and help constrain relative gap phases. A matrix eigenvalue is not the arithmetic sum of all its entries. The energy cutoff notation here makes the dimensions explicit when converting the original ASCII equation. [R1](#ref-source-e6ac5c48a0e11fe3)

The full problem can have different frequency spectra, momentum structure, repulsive terms, Coulomb effects and normal self-energy renormalization. Combining a pairing attraction and a mass enhancement into one positive scalar can give a misleading temperature estimate. Interactions can cooperate, compete or favor different gap structures after projection into the pairing channel. [R3](#ref-source-d7ac492f79e0915b)

## Experimental criteria

Resolve gap magnitudes and their band assignments with complementary spectroscopy and thermodynamics. State the band or orbital basis, energy cutoff, Coulomb treatment and disorder model. Distinguish a measurement that observes two gaps from an inference that identifies two different mediating bosons. Normal-state two-component Drude fits do not by themselves establish two superconducting gaps.

MgB2 provides a benchmark: the discovery report established a transition near 39 K, and anisotropic first-principles Eliashberg calculations addressed different gaps on sigma and pi bands. Two gaps in this setting do not require two unrelated pairing glues. Quantitative comparison depends on the actual band-resolved calculation and sample, not a coupling budget borrowed from another compound. [R2](#ref-source-fade6558e7eafb2b) [R3](#ref-source-d7ac492f79e0915b)

## Material interpretation

In single-layer FeSe/SrTiO3, replica-band observations support the relevance of an interface electron-phonon interaction. They do not independently extract every spin, interface and plasmon contribution as a set of additive coupling constants. The interface hypothesis must be tested together with charge transfer, the reconstructed electronic structure and phase-coherence limitations. [R4](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc)

A high pairing or gap-closing scale measured by ARPES is not automatically a zero-resistance transition. When an interface and intrinsic electronic interactions are both discussed, the useful object is a specified combined kernel with assumptions and uncertainties. This pilot deliberately contains no unsourced table of separate FeSe/SrTiO3 coupling constants. [R4](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc)

## Limits and disputes

A common transition temperature is compatible with interband locking, but does not establish beneficial synergy between distinct interactions. Changes in a band structure, density of states or scattering rate can alter the instability without revealing a unique mediator. Cross-material percentages assigned to a plasmon enhancement are not universal physical constants. [R1](#ref-source-e6ac5c48a0e11fe3) [R3](#ref-source-d7ac492f79e0915b)

## Discovery implications

A testable multichannel proposal predicts a gap structure and its response to an independent control parameter. Show what would distinguish cooperation from competition, and check that the same interaction has not been counted twice. The most useful next measurement constrains a specific matrix element or spectral contribution rather than simply adding another possible mechanism to a list. [R1](#ref-source-e6ac5c48a0e11fe3) [R3](#ref-source-d7ac492f79e0915b)

## Related topics

See [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [iron-based materials](/scwiki/iron-based-superconductors), and [two-dimensional interfaces](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces).

articles.body:
## Scope

The label s± describes a superconducting gap whose sign differs between relevant Fermi-surface sheets. In common iron-based models the state belongs to the fully symmetric A1g representation, while different pockets carry opposite gap signs. A fully open gap therefore does not establish a sign-preserving state. The precise pocket and orbital assignments must come from the actual material rather than a generic two-pocket drawing. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

## Mathematical assumptions

A minimal illustration is

$
\Delta_h=+\Delta_1,\qquad
\Delta_e=-\Delta_2.
$

The labels $h$ and $e$ refer to hole and electron pockets in the model, not to a universal inventory present in every iron-based superconductor. Repulsive interband scattering can favor opposite signs in a linearized pairing equation. Mazin and colleagues and Kuroki and colleagues developed important iron-based proposals, but their predictions depend on the Fermi surface and interaction assumptions. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

An A1g gap can also be anisotropic and can develop accidental nodes. This possibility should be distinguished from symmetry-enforced nodes in another representation. Observing nodes alone cannot choose among every candidate, and no one compound determines the gap of an entire family. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

## Experimental criteria

A neutron resonance can be consistent with a sign-changing coherence factor, but its interpretation depends on the normal-state response and gap structure. Christianson and colleagues studied K-doped Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2; the pinned chapter's Co-doped attribution is corrected here. Their result provides a material-specific constraint rather than a universal direct phase measurement. [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3)

Quasiparticle interference depends on scattering channels, matrix elements, field conditions and a band model. Hanaguri and colleagues' Fe(Se,Te) study is not a measurement on pure bulk FeSe, and its evidence should not be paraphrased as directly photographing a negative gap sign. Complementary phase-sensitive junctions, controlled disorder studies and gap spectroscopy can narrow alternatives. [R4](#ref-source-3ee65ce8fc5080da)

## Corrected nodal example

Reid and colleagues' 2012 thermal-conductivity paper, DOI 10.1103/PhysRevLett.109.087001, is about KFe2As2. The authors report residual heat transport consistent with nodes and argue for a d-wave interpretation. It is not a P-substituted Ba122 paper. The previous attribution is corrected in the source mapping and in the register for C2 and C10. No replacement P-Ba122 claim is silently inferred from this DOI. [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

This correction matters physically: a source arguing for symmetry-imposed nodes cannot be repurposed as a demonstration of accidental nodes in another compound. The editorial record preserves the original path and hash so readers can identify what changed. [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

## Limits and disputes

FeSe, shallow-band systems, strongly hole-doped endpoints and electron-only interfaces can require models different from the original hole-electron-pocket proposal. A candidate s± solution for a nickelate is a theoretical proposal until an appropriate experiment constrains it. Gap magnitude, gap sign, nodes and the microscopic pairing interaction are separate inference steps. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

## Discovery implications

Specify which sheets are expected to change sign and what observation could reject that assignment. Use measured electronic structure, compare several independent probes and retain sample composition. For agent retrieval, quote the claim together with the named material and source; the sign structure is not an unconditional property of the phrase “iron-based superconductor.” [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R4](#ref-source-3ee65ce8fc5080da) [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

## Related topics

Continue with [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), [iron-based superconductors](/scwiki/iron-based-superconductors), and [nickelate materials](/scwiki/nickelates).

articles.body:
## Scope

Two-dimensional geometry and interface location are different coordinates. A film can have weak out-of-plane electronic dispersion without displaying a clean two-dimensional phase transition. An interface can host a superconducting region even when its two constituents are not superconducting alone. Neither statement identifies one universal mechanism for increasing a critical temperature. [R1](#ref-source-ea5d0c80335c450d) [R2](#ref-source-684b96e9dbb65a64)

An interface may change charge transfer, oxygen defects, strain, orbital structure, phonons and disorder at the same time. Pair formation and macroscopic phase coherence can also occur at different scales. A useful report states whether a temperature comes from a spectral gap, resistive onset, zero resistance, magnetic screening or a BKT analysis. [R4](#ref-source-a95bcf0cb2681557) [R5](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc) [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Mathematical assumptions

For an ideal two-dimensional phase model, the BKT universal jump can be written in an energy-stiffness convention as

$
k_BT_{\mathrm{BKT}}=\frac{\pi}{2}J_s(T_{\mathrm{BKT}}^-).
$

Here $J_s$ is the renormalized total phase stiffness immediately below the transition. The normalization and the relevant long-wavelength limit must be stated. The relation does not apply directly to a bare mean-field pairing amplitude, and it does not separately measure a geometric contribution to the total stiffness. Finite size, inhomogeneity and interlayer coupling can modify an experimental comparison. [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

BCS-like amplitude formation and BKT-like phase ordering describe different aspects of a system. Treating them as mutually exclusive microscopic pairing mechanisms would confuse an interaction model with a phase-coherence transition. [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Experimental criteria

Combine independent phase-sensitive observables rather than fitting one resistive tail. Test non-linear current-voltage behavior, a suitable fluctuation-transport regime and sheet stiffness where available. Check finite-size effects, heating, current range and measurement frequency. A large anisotropy of the upper critical field is not by itself a BKT proof.

At LaAlO3/SrTiO3, Reyren and colleagues reported an interface transition around 200 mK with two-dimensional behavior. The source's inferred superconducting thickness is an upper bound, not an exact directly imaged electronic width. Gating can tune an interface phase diagram without proving that carrier density is its only control parameter. [R1](#ref-source-ea5d0c80335c450d)

## Interface examples

Cuprate heterostructures constructed from non-superconducting components demonstrate that an interface can support superconductivity. Gozar and colleagues and the layer-selective work of Logvenov and colleagues constrain where the superconducting response occurs. They establish particular interface states rather than the claim that interlayer coupling is irrelevant to every high-temperature cuprate. [R2](#ref-source-684b96e9dbb65a64) [R3](#ref-source-7fcd7faadf66481b)

For single-layer FeSe/SrTiO3, a roughly 65 ± 5 K ARPES pairing scale retains its spectroscopic label. Replica-band evidence supports an interface electron-phonon interaction, but does not quantify every contribution to the full pairing kernel. This number cannot satisfy a query requiring zero resistance, even though it is a valid temperature observation. [R4](#ref-source-a95bcf0cb2681557) [R5](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc)

## Limits and disputes

A dome-shaped gate dependence does not uniquely identify a quantum critical pairing interaction. Ionic gating also needs electrochemical controls. A superconducting single layer shows that one layer can suffice under the reported conditions, not that dimensionality or interlayer coupling never matters. Interface improvements should not be merged with bulk or transient temperature records. [R1](#ref-source-ea5d0c80335c450d) [R3](#ref-source-7fcd7faadf66481b) [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Discovery implications

Plan controls that separate thickness, interface termination, oxygen, strain and electrostatics. Report sample-to-sample variation alongside the most favorable device. A mechanism becomes more useful when it predicts which independent interface modification should change a gap scale and which should change phase stiffness. Keep those two outcomes separate in both the narrative and structured evidence. [R5](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc) [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Related topics

See [transport evidence](/scwiki/zero-resistance), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [geometric stiffness](/scwiki/geometric-superfluid-weight).

articles.body:
## Scope

Cuprates share CuO2 planes as a central electronic motif, but they do not share one complete phase diagram. Layer count, apical oxygen, charge-reservoir blocks, disorder and the sign and amount of doping vary across families. The La-Ba-Cu-O discovery and the subsequent Y-Ba-Cu-O work established the high-temperature cuprate research platform; they do not make every later composition equivalent. [R1](#ref-source-ad4ee05105f93caf) [R2](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e)

Many parent compounds are antiferromagnetic correlated insulators. Doping can produce superconductivity together with pseudogap behavior, charge correlations and unusual normal-state transport. A schematic dome is an organizing picture rather than a universal quantitative equation for all compounds. A weak-coupling phonon-only explanation is not a complete account of the family, while Cooper pairing and broken-symmetry descriptions remain useful. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

## Mathematical assumptions

A frequently used illustrative form of a two-dimensional d-wave gap is

$
\Delta(\mathbf k)\propto\cos k_x-\cos k_y.
$

This lattice expression represents a symmetry structure in an appropriate square-lattice description. It is not a fit to every Fermi surface, and it does not specify a pairing mediator or an absolute gap magnitude. The significance of a sign change must be connected to phase-sensitive and momentum-resolved evidence in the named material. [R5](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7) [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

## Experimental criteria

Keep a transport onset, zero-resistance point, magnetic response and thermodynamic anomaly in separate fields. Record pressure, medium, oxygen content, preparation route and sample form. For a gap-symmetry claim, combine phase-sensitive tests with complementary spectroscopy and low-energy response. Tricrystal experiments provide an important phase-sensitive cuprate constraint; their interpretation should not be extended automatically to every electron-doped, highly disordered or pressure-treated sample. [R5](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7)

The familiar Hg-1223 examples illustrate the danger of unconditioned comparisons: the historical ambient-pressure transition near 133 K and a high-pressure scale near 164 K around 31 GPa concern different conditions. The pilot leaves an individual onset-versus-zero criterion unknown where this scoped review has not re-extracted it. That missing field must not be silently supplied by a search or an agent. [R3](#ref-source-d95477ebe515f481) [R4](#ref-source-6d09a24a26a15997)

## Limits and disputes

Antiferromagnetic correlations, a pseudogap and charge order constrain a microscopic theory without selecting one unique pairing glue. A charge-density modulation is not by itself evidence of a pair-density wave. Likewise, a linear-temperature resistivity is not an automatic measurement of a Planckian scattering time. The observable and the inference must remain separate. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

The source chapter includes a 2026 pressure-quench report and distinguishes an onset from zero resistance. Its new quantitative claims have not received a primary-text check in this pilot and are not included as verified comparison records. Metastable pressure-treated material must remain distinct from an equilibrium ambient-pressure phase. The omission and review limitation are preserved in the editorial mapping.

## Discovery implications

A useful mechanism predicts more than a plausible energy scale: it should connect an interaction model to gap symmetry, a material trend and a falsifiable observation. Spin-fluctuation, RVB and lattice-related approaches have different assumptions and outstanding tests. Treat their coexistence in a review as competing explanations, not a combined proof. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

## Related topics

See [magnetic evidence](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [spin-liquid and RVB proposals](/scwiki/spin-liquids-and-superconductivity), and [Planckian transport](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation).

articles.body:
## Scope

Iron-based superconductors include Fe-pnictogen and Fe-chalcogen layers in several structural families. Their low-energy electronic structure commonly involves several Fe 3d orbitals. Many parent compounds are metallic with coupled magnetic, structural or nematic order; this is a different starting point from a simple single-band cuprate analogy. Kamihara and colleagues' F-doped 1111 material established the early high-temperature platform. [R1](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7)

Distinguish 1111, 122, 111 and 11 materials, and treat a single-layer interface separately from a bulk crystal. The K-doped 122 superconductor reported by Rotter and colleagues is not the undoped BaFe2As2 parent. The discovery of superconductivity in FeSe likewise does not imply that its excess-Fe content or electronic structure can be ignored. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e) [R3](#ref-source-205024adeb431322)

## Mathematical assumptions

A multiband description uses gaps $\Delta_i(\mathbf k)$ on a measured set of bands or orbitals. A candidate s± solution has a relative sign between appropriate Fermi-surface sheets. It is a pairing-model result, not a consequence of the material containing iron. Changes in Fermi surfaces, shallow bands or orbital weights can change which candidate is favored. [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

Doping notation also needs care. The numerical coefficient $x$ in $\mathrm{BaFe}_{2-x}\mathrm{Co}_x\mathrm{As}_2$ differs from the fraction $x$ in $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x}\mathrm{Co}_x)_2\mathrm{As}_2$. Comparing “optimal x” values without converting their definitions can manufacture a disagreement. This pilot avoids a universal optimum or a universal orbital-coupling table.

## Experimental criteria

Report structural family, composition, sample form, preparation and pressure with each superconducting observation. Separate a parent magnetic or structural transition from a superconducting transition in a substituted compound. State whether a temperature is an onset, zero resistance, bulk response or spectroscopic gap scale. Unknown criteria remain unknown in the structured records.

The Fe1.01Se pressure result is a concrete condition check: the cited report associates 36.7 K with 8.9 GPa, not an unqualified 1-2 GPa result. That value cannot be copied into an ambient-pressure materials entry. Formula and pressure accompany it in the HTML and API record. [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b)

## Evidence for gap structure

The superconductivity-induced neutron response of Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2 constrains sign-changing pairing models. It does not directly determine the gaps of all 1111, 122, FeSe or interface systems. A synthesis should state the measured wave vector, normal-state spectrum and candidate coherence-factor interpretation. [R5](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

For an interface, replica bands or a high ARPES gap-closing scale must retain their spectroscopic labels. A reconstructed single-layer Fermi surface may differ substantially from the canonical hole-electron-pocket model. This is why the interface article and the multiband article are separate from a bulk-family temperature comparison. [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

## Limits and disputes

Several orbitals and strong correlations provide useful organizing language, but they do not establish a universal pairing mechanism. Hund-related mass renormalization is not automatically a larger pairing eigenvalue. FeSe, strongly doped endpoints and interface systems are especially important tests of simple family-wide statements. A strong evidence chain for a candidate gap is different from a unique microscopic verdict. [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

## Discovery implications

Use controlled changes in structure, composition, strain and disorder to test a specific model. Preserve the distinction between modifying a Fermi surface and identifying the boson that pairs electrons. The most useful database entry is a condition-rich measurement linked to its original compound, not one universal iron-based critical temperature. [R1](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7) [R3](#ref-source-205024adeb431322) [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b)

## Related topics

Read [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [two-dimensional interfaces](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces).

## Scope

“Nickelate superconductivity” includes distinct structural and preparation routes. Infinite-layer RNiO2 films and bilayer Ruddlesden-Popper La3Ni2O7 crystals differ in layer geometry, oxygen coordination and electronic structure. Their temperatures should not be presented as continuous optimization of one material. Li and colleagues' 2019 discovery and Sun and colleagues' 2023 high-pressure report establish different experimental settings. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

The infinite-layer route uses epitaxial precursors and topotactic reduction. Oxygen stoichiometry, residual apical oxygen, reduction uniformity and the substrate can all matter. A nominal chemical formula does not prove identical electronic states across bulk powders, supported films and membranes. This pilot does not infer a universal exchange energy or a common one-band model from the resemblance of NiO2 and CuO2 planes. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

## Mathematical assumptions

An orbital label such as $d_{x^2-y^2}$ or $d_{z^2}$ identifies part of a model basis; it does not by itself identify the pairing channel. A proposed gap or coupling matrix needs a declared band structure, filling, interaction and structural phase. Similar local configurations can motivate a cuprate analogy, but do not transfer a phase diagram or a numerical pairing scale to nickelates. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

Pressure changes can involve structural rearrangement as well as electronic bandwidth. For a bilayer crystal, a model evaluated in one structural phase must be compared with measurements in the same pressure regime. Distinguish calculations suggesting a favorable orbital configuration from observations establishing superconducting signatures. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## Experimental criteria

Record family, layer count, rare-earth composition, sample form, reduction procedure, oxygen content and substrate. Keep resistance onset, zero resistance, magnetic response and superconducting fraction separate. If a field-induced or re-entrant state is proposed, include field direction and the temperature of the measurement rather than substituting a characteristic field for an upper critical field.

The Li source reports a transition range around 9-15 K in infinite-layer films. This pilot does not assign precise onset and zero values without re-extracting those individual criteria. The Sun abstract reports a maximum scale of 80 K in La3Ni2O7 over pressures between 14.0 and 43.5 GPa with resistance and susceptibility evidence. The maximum is not asserted to occur at every pressure in that interval. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## Limits and disputes

An 80 K high-pressure bilayer observation is not ambient-pressure bulk superconductivity. Likewise, a strained film and a pressure-treated crystal need not follow an identical structural path. The 2026 film, membrane, oxygen-cycling and magnetic-substitution updates in the pinned chapter require separate primary-text checks. This pilot retains their review debt rather than adding their numbers to a quantitative record. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853) [R3](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9)

The pairing symmetry and microscopic interaction remain inference questions. A theoretical s± candidate, an orbital-selective interpretation or a magnetic compensation scenario must keep its theoretical or hypothetical label until supported by the corresponding phase-sensitive or field-resolved evidence. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## Discovery implications

Compare controlled sample series within a structural family before making cross-family claims. A useful design experiment separates oxygen, strain, interface and carrier changes as far as possible. Negative controls are especially valuable when two substrates both produce compression but only one preparation yields a transition. Such observations constrain a mechanism without proving that one structural variable is sufficient. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R3](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9)

articles.body:
## Scope

Strain is a directional deformation relative to a stated reference structure. Epitaxial clamping, uniaxial loading and hydrostatic pressure impose different constraints, so “compressive” does not specify a unique path through a material's phase diagram. A thin film also carries substrate, defect and oxygen-history variables that a bulk pressure experiment does not reproduce automatically. [R1](#ref-source-363388aa03563c00) [R2](#ref-source-2c98c9257f2c4d46)

This article treats the mechanical control and its evidential limits. A changed transition temperature is an observation; the attribution of that change to a particular bond angle, orbital or fluctuation is a further inference. Strain is useful precisely because it can tune selected directions, but the experimental boundary conditions must be retained. [R1](#ref-source-363388aa03563c00) [R3](#ref-source-c9a97c501c718b62)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a lattice parameter $a$ relative to a relaxed reference $a_0$, an engineering strain is

$
\epsilon=\frac{a-a_0}{a_0}.
$

A nominal coherent epitaxial mismatch may be written

$
f=\frac{a_{\mathrm{sub}}-a_{\mathrm{ref}}}{a_{\mathrm{ref}}}.
$

The nominal mismatch is not automatically the measured strain in a partially relaxed film. Dislocations, domains and thickness-dependent relaxation can change the actual lattice parameters. State the reference phase, orientation and measurement temperature rather than assigning one strain percentage from a substrate name. [R1](#ref-source-363388aa03563c00)

In a small-deformation continuum description, the strain tensor is the symmetric displacement gradient. Hydrostatic stress has the form $\sigma_{ij}=-p\delta_{ij}$, whereas uniaxial and epitaxial boundary conditions select directions. The resulting strain also depends on the elastic response. Out-of-plane expansion under in-plane compression is therefore not a contradiction. [R1](#ref-source-363388aa03563c00)

## Experimental criteria

Measure actual lattice deformation using an appropriate structural method and report calibration, loading direction, transverse response, relaxation and hysteresis. Keep nominal mismatch and measured strain in separate fields. For superconductivity, identify onset, zero resistance or a magnetic/thermodynamic criterion, and compare equivalent sample histories.

In Sr2RuO4, the earlier Hicks study and the later higher-strain Steppke study are distinct experimental steps. The larger transition-temperature peak belongs to the latter; it should not be attributed to the initial apparatus or to the earlier paper without checking the original curve. The pilot preserves an approximate source-reported scale while explicitly leaving an unretrieved criterion unknown. [R2](#ref-source-2c98c9257f2c4d46) [R3](#ref-source-c9a97c501c718b62)

## Limits and disputes

A peak in transition temperature near a reconstructed Fermi surface is a constraint on theory, not a determination of every pairing property. Orbital shifts, density-of-states changes and modified correlations can coexist. Inferring a pairing symmetry still requires complementary measurements. [R3](#ref-source-c9a97c501c718b62)

The pinned chapter's 2026 nickelate-film discussion distinguishes nominal and measured mismatch and warns against assuming that in-plane compression requires a shorter c axis. That update has not received a primary-text check here. Its strain percentages and transition values are consequently not promoted into the pilot's quantitative record. Oxygen stoichiometry, interface structure and defects remain possible covariates, not solved nuisance parameters. [R4](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9)

## Discovery implications

Prefer controlled series that change one mechanical coordinate while monitoring oxygen, microstructure and sample geometry. A substrate series alone may change several variables at once. A useful design proposal predicts a trend, a null control and an independent structural or spectroscopic response, rather than stating that more compression must always improve superconductivity. [R1](#ref-source-363388aa03563c00) [R3](#ref-source-c9a97c501c718b62)

## Related topics

See [nickelate structures](/scwiki/nickelates), [interface superconductivity](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces), and [cuprate comparisons](/scwiki/cuprates).

For a lattice parameter $a$ relative to a relaxed reference $a_0$, an engineering strain is

$
\epsilon=\frac{a-a_0}{a_0}.

A nominal coherent epitaxial mismatch may be written

$
f=\frac{a_{\mathrm{sub}}-a_{\mathrm{ref}}}{a_{\mathrm{ref}}}.

Hydrostatic stress has the form $\sigma_{ij}=-p\delta_{ij}$, whereas uniaxial and epitaxial boundary conditions select directions. The resulting strain also depends on the elastic response. articles.body:
## Scope

Superfluid weight describes the response of a superconducting system to a phase twist or electromagnetic field in a specified limiting procedure. In multiband systems the current response can include a contribution related to Bloch-state geometry, beyond the conventional dispersion-related part. Peotta and Törmä developed an important flat-band formulation; subsequent work extended the multiband description. [R1](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

The phrase “interband contribution” concerns response matrix elements. It does not require the assertion that every Cooper pair contains one electron from each of two different bands, and it does not mean that an experiment has isolated two separately flowing currents. Definitions of superfluid weight, sheet stiffness and penetration depth can differ by charge, Planck-constant, thickness and normalization factors. [R1](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

## Mathematical assumptions

Within a stated multiband mean-field response convention, write

$
D_{s,ij}=D^{\mathrm{conv}}_{ij}+D^{\mathrm{geom}}_{ij}.
$

A useful schematic form in an isolated-band, uniform-pairing limit is

$
D^{\mathrm{geom}}_{ij}\propto
\sum_{\mathbf k}\frac{|\Delta|^2}{E_{\mathbf k}}
\tanh\!\left(\frac{E_{\mathbf k}}{2k_BT}\right)g_{ij}(\mathbf k).
$

This proportionality displays the quantum-metric structure. It is not a numerical formula without the Hamiltonian, degeneracy, Brillouin-zone normalization and electromagnetic prefactor. For a normalized isolated Bloch state, the metric can be defined as

$
g_{ij}=\operatorname{Re}\langle\partial_i u|
(1-|u\rangle\langle u|)|\partial_j u\rangle.
$

The isolated-band and self-consistency assumptions are consequential, especially near small interband gaps or nonuniform order parameters. [R1](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

## Experimental criteria

State which stiffness convention is measured, its units, dimensionality, thickness and frequency regime. Preserve the order of static and long-wavelength limits. To claim a geometric fraction, compare a justified multiband calculation with a conventional baseline and the measured total response. Measuring a total value larger than one simple estimate motivates further modeling; it is not a model-free subtraction. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R4](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

For a BKT comparison, use the renormalized total phase stiffness in the appropriate sheet-energy convention. A transition temperature can constrain that total without separately measuring the geometric term. The relation between pairing amplitude and phase coherence remains a second issue. [R1](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

## Limits and disputes

Topology can impose a lower bound under particular assumptions, but a nonzero Chern number is not necessary for geometric superfluid weight. A Chern-trivial band can still have a nonzero quantum metric. Lieb-lattice work is a useful model example of finite flat-band superfluid response. The result is theoretical and depends on its interaction and band assumptions. [R1](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R2](#ref-source-b43340ce5c356e49)

A positive geometric contribution is not a guarantee that an experimental critical temperature equals a mean-field pairing scale. Disorder, remote-band truncation, self-consistent order-parameter response and phase fluctuations affect quantitative comparisons. The moire experiment cited in the source chapter supplies an important constraint, but this pilot has not reanalyzed its raw data or independently separated a geometric fraction. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R4](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

## Discovery implications

Use geometry as a calculable constraint rather than an attractive label for a flat band. Report conventional, geometric and total response together, test the band truncation and state which prediction can be checked independently. A large metric does not compensate automatically for poor pairing, unfavorable filling or loss of macroscopic coherence. [R1](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

## Related topics

Compare [magnetic penetration-depth evidence](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [two-dimensional phase coherence](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces), and [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing).

articles.body:
## Scope

A quantum spin liquid is a proposed quantum many-body state, not simply a material with no detected magnetic order. Real candidate systems require tests that distinguish persistent quantum behavior from glassiness, valence-bond order, disorder and a measurement window that is not yet cold or slow enough. A claim about fractionalization is stronger than an observation of missing magnetic Bragg peaks. [R2](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R4](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

RVB, or resonating valence bond, provides a family of theoretical constructions using superpositions of spin-singlet configurations. Anderson's cuprate proposal connected this language to doped correlated insulators. It remains a mechanism proposal rather than a proof that an undoped cuprate parent is an experimentally established spin liquid. In particular, the antiferromagnetic parent-state evidence cannot be replaced by a preferred wavefunction picture. [R1](#ref-source-5a6026d6455bf7a0)

## Mathematical assumptions

A schematic singlet-covering state can be written

$
|\Psi_{\mathrm{RVB}}\rangle
=\sum_C A_C\prod_{(i,j)\in C}
\frac{|\uparrow_i\downarrow_j\rangle-|\downarrow_i\uparrow_j\rangle}{\sqrt{2}}.
$

The amplitudes $A_C$, allowed coverings and constraints define the actual variational state. This expression alone does not establish its normalization, topological order or suitability for a particular material. Different parton and gauge constructions can yield different phases; a generic U(1) state should not automatically be called a Dirac state. [R1](#ref-source-5a6026d6455bf7a0)

Likewise, singlet correlations do not demonstrate superconductivity. A charged coherent condensate, an insulating spin system and a variational pairing amplitude are distinct physical objects. BCS mean-field language can organize pairing beyond a phonon-only interaction, so a simple “BCS versus RVB” dichotomy hides assumptions rather than testing them. [R1](#ref-source-5a6026d6455bf7a0)

## Experimental criteria

State the temperature floor, field, time window and probe used to exclude magnetic order or freezing. Compare local magnetic probes with thermodynamics, transport and structural controls. A low-temperature heat-capacity term or a continuum of excitations can be informative, but each has alternative explanations and sample dependencies. Do not use one such feature as a complete topological-state diagnosis. [R2](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R4](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

The organic compound kappa-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3 is an important candidate platform. Shimizu and colleagues reported a lack of conventional order to low temperatures, while the pressure work of Kurosaki and colleagues mapped neighboring electronic phases. These are separate observations: the pressure-induced superconducting region does not show that the insulating state's proposed fractionalized excitations are the pairing mediator. [R2](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R3](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c)

## Limits and disputes

The candidate interpretation has continuing spin-gap and valence-bond-order questions, explicitly represented by the later source cited here. Pressure changes bandwidth and may change several effective parameters. A neighboring superconductor is therefore evidence of phase-diagram proximity, not a controlled demonstration of a QSL-to-superconductor microscopic route. [R3](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c) [R4](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

Frustration is a useful route to suppressing simple order, but it is neither sufficient nor a universal necessary condition for every spin-liquid construction. Different topological labels and proposed excitations must be tied to a specified theoretical state. The pilot removes categorical material assignments and universal heat-capacity exponents from the original overview. [R1](#ref-source-5a6026d6455bf7a0) [R4](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

## Discovery implications

A testable proposal should predict a controlled change in fractionalization-sensitive and charge-coherence observables across a transition. Preserve negative evidence and disorder diagnostics. The strongest research lead is a mechanism-specific discriminating measurement, not the co-occurrence of superconductivity and a suggestive insulating phase diagram. [R2](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R3](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c)

## Related topics

Read [cuprate evidence](/scwiki/cuprates), [gap-sign constraints](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), and [normal-state dissipation](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation).

articles.body:
## Scope

“Planckian” commonly describes a specified relaxation rate on the scale $k_BT/\hbar$, with a dimensionless coefficient of order unity. It is not a theorem inferred from a resistivity curve that happens to be linear in temperature. Transport, optical, single-particle, thermalization and quantum-chaos times probe different correlation functions and need not be equal. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

A useful experimental statement names the channel, fitting range and assumptions. It also separates an empirical scale from a proposed universal bound. The phrase “of order one” must not become an exact $\alpha=1$ assertion without uncertainties and a consistent convention. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029) [R2](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a specified transport lifetime, a total dimensionless ratio is

$
\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}(T)=\frac{\hbar}{k_BT\,\tau_{\mathrm{tr}}(T)}.
$

A model with a residual rate can instead be parametrized as

$
\frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{tr}}(T)}
=\frac{1}{\tau_0}+\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}\frac{k_BT}{\hbar}.
$

The second coefficient describes the inelastic slope under this assumption; it is not the first ratio when a residual term is appreciable. This distinction is made explicit in converting the source's ASCII notation. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

In a single-band Drude limit with temperature-independent effective inputs,

$
\rho=\frac{m^\ast}{ne^2\tau_{\mathrm{tr}}},\qquad
\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}
=\frac{\hbar}{k_B}\frac{ne^2}{m^\ast}\frac{d\rho}{dT}.
$

The resistivity slope alone does not supply the carrier density $n$ or transport mass $m^\ast$. Multiband conduction, changing spectral weight, angular scattering and vertex effects can invalidate this simple inversion. Sheet resistance and bulk resistivity must also use consistent thickness conventions. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029) [R2](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae)

## Experimental criteria

Specify the lifetime definition, residual subtraction, frequency convention, fitting interval and uncertainties. State whether a quoted rate is an angular frequency or ordinary frequency; confusing $h$ with $\hbar$ introduces a factor of $2\pi$. Use independent optical or Fermi-surface constraints where available, and propagate their uncertainty into an inferred coefficient.

Bruin and colleagues compared inferred rates across metals, while Legros and colleagues examined overdoped cuprates with a per-plane scaling analysis. Those studies provide important constraints within their transport assumptions. They do not measure one exact universal coefficient for every composition and every relaxation channel. [R2](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae) [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

## Limits and disputes

Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford bound the growth of a regularized out-of-time-order correlator by $\lambda_L\leq 2\pi k_BT/\hbar$. Their argument assumes analyticity and boundedness in a thermal complex-time strip, controlled factorization errors, and a separation between dissipation and scrambling times. It constrains a quantum-chaos exponent, not a measured charge-transport relaxation rate. Identifying $\lambda_L$ with $1/\tau_{\mathrm{tr}}$ requires additional model-specific justification; the bound does not establish a universal transport coefficient $\alpha=1$. [R5](#ref-source-8339743a9f1c3239) [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

The pinned chapter includes a 2026 FeTeSe frequency-domain report and a slow/fast-channel interpretation. That source's detailed sample and fitting claims are not independently re-extracted in this pilot. They are not used to prove a pairing mediator or to validate a separate multichannel theory. A fitted normal-state channel and a superconducting gap are different evidence objects. [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Discovery implications

Use a Planckian-scale observation to formulate a falsifiable normal-state model. Ask which spectral weight, carrier estimate and scattering anisotropy would support or reject the proposed interpretation. Proximity to superconductivity can motivate a mechanism study, but it does not establish that faster scattering raises the critical temperature. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029) [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

## Related topics

See [zero-resistance evidence](/scwiki/zero-resistance), [iron-based materials](/scwiki/iron-based-superconductors), and [spin-liquid proposals](/scwiki/spin-liquids-and-superconductivity).
